title: Scaling Training Workloads
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of scaling training workloads in a PyTorch workflow.
Apply a small example of scaling training workloads and interpret the output.
Identify a relevant limitation, debugging check, or reproducibility concern.

content.intro: Scaling Training Workloads: Distributed training coordinates multiple processes, devices, or machines. DataParallel-style replication and sharded strategies trade memory, communication, and operational complexity differently. In this lesson, use a small example to make the inputs, outputs, and boundary conditions explicit.
content.why_it_matters: Scaling may make a model fit or training finish sooner, but communication and coordination can outweigh the benefit on small workloads. For this lesson, focus on global versus local batch size and the evidence you can collect from a controlled example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Understand ranks, process groups, collective operations, sampler behavior, rank-aware output, and checkpoint ownership before launching multi-process training. The source topics for this lesson are: Global versus local batch size, Learning-rate considerations, Throughput and scaling efficiency. Keep each topic connected to a checkable input/output behavior.

content_blocks.title: Read the example
content_blocks.text: Separate the local computation from communication and note which process owns logging or checkpoint writes. Use torchrun only in an intentionally configured process environment. The example is a teaching-scale check, not evidence of a trained model score or a hardware-independent performance claim.

items.title: Global versus local batch size
items.text: Inspect one sample before batching, verify feature/label alignment, and confirm that preprocessing and split boundaries fit the intended stage.

items.title: Learning-rate considerations
items.text: Connect this topic to the lesson workflow: Understand ranks, process groups, collective operations, sampler behavior, rank-aware output, and checkpoint ownership before launching multi-process training. Write down the expected behavior and test it on a small, inspectable input.

items.title: Throughput and scaling efficiency
items.text: Measure a representative baseline with warm-up and repeated trials, change one factor, and re-check output quality before claiming improvement.

items.text: Record the artifact state and environment assumptions, restore it in a clean model, and verify behavior on a fixed input before trusting the result.

content.task: Try it yourself: Draw a single-node two-rank data/gradient flow and document the launch command, backend, data-sampler, and checkpoint responsibilities. Record the observed result and one limitation; do not report an unrun training or performance result as measured.

troubleshooting.symptom: A tensor operation raises a shape, dtype, or device mismatch.
troubleshooting.check: Print .shape, .dtype, and .device for each input. Resolve the mismatch intentionally instead of changing dimensions blindly.

troubleshooting.symptom: The example fails because an optional package or accelerator is unavailable.
troubleshooting.check: Check the installed PyTorch/package versions and device availability. Use the official installation selector and run the CPU-compatible path where appropriate.

troubleshooting.symptom: The result differs across runs or machines.
troubleshooting.check: Fix the seed where useful, record versions and inputs, and document operations that remain nondeterministic or hardware dependent.

common_mistakes.problem: Relying on assumptions instead of inspecting the data or output.
common_mistakes.why: Many ML failures come from incorrect shapes, labels, preprocessing, or execution mode rather than a syntax error.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect representative inputs and add assertions for the expected shape, dtype, range, or behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing training-time behavior with inference-time behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Dropout, normalization, gradient tracking, and optimizer updates can change how a model behaves.
common_mistakes.fix: Do not run a DDP script as an ordinary single Python process without its required distributed initialization.

common_mistakes.problem: Using a current or experimental API without recording its version assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Hardware support and ecosystem APIs can change independently of the core package.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin compatible dependencies, record the environment, and test after upgrades.
